name: Gareth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say here stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm out of the depot on Mill Road by seven, six if there's been wind overnight. We're a four-man distribution crew covering the hill farms and the villages up the valley, so it's mostly pole changes, broken crossarms, a transformer that's cooked itself, and the odd tractor that's backed into a stay wire. I've been on the lines about seven years now, apprenticeship included.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that when we leave, the lights are on. You get an old farmer coming out with tea because his freezers are full of lamb and he's been dark for nine hours, and that feels good. What wears me out is the money, honestly. I'm on the lower end of the pay scale for this work, Rosa's at the care home on nights, and after rent on our flat there's maybe a few hundred left at the end of the month, if the van doesn't need tyres.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is there other line work nearby if you wanted to move?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not really. There's our company and that's it for seventy kilometres. The contractors come in after big storms and then they leave again. So you hang on to the job you've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, that it's a lot of noise from people in offices. At work the lads would joke that the chatbot still can't climb a pole. Online I don't really post, I just read the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. I don't use any of that stuff, I don't want to, and if it stays a toy for office people then my job looks like my job. The bigger problem for me is still pay, and AI doesn't fix that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep turning up, keep my head down, try to get on the standby rota more because callouts pay time and a half. I'd probably push at the union meeting for the pay review again, but that's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Like reading a forecast that says no storm this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the money is the real pressure. Which bill is hardest each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van, because the depot is twenty minutes away and there's no bus at six in the morning. Last winter the clutch went and that was most of a month's spare cash gone in one afternoon. Robots aren't what keeps me up. A clutch is what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything AI could do at the depot that you'd actually welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the paperwork. We fill in a job sheet, a risk sheet and a switching log for every fault, and half of it's the same thing three times. If a computer did that and nobody lost their job over it, fine. But I'd still want a person checking the switching, because a mistake there kills someone.

S0.say: It's mostly noise from people in offices, and the chatbot still can't climb a pole. I don't post about it, I just read the union page and get on with the job.
S0.think: It'd be a relief, because I don't use AI and don't want to. My real pressure is low pay and the cost of keeping a van running, and AI doesn't change that.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and tries to get more standby shifts, since callouts pay time and a half. Raises the pay review again at the next union meeting.
S0.feel: Calm, close to relieved. The money worry is still there, but it has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: Robots aren't what keeps me up. A clutch is what keeps me up.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth's anxiety is real but it's about wages and his old van, not technology. He'd accept AI doing duplicate paperwork, but draws a hard line at switching, which he sees as life or death. He is a quiet union man rather than a loud one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be at the union meeting saying we need it in writing: no drone replaces a crew, and nobody's let go because of new kit. I'd tell my mates down the pub to join if they haven't. Online I'd share the union's stuff, but I wouldn't write my own posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd use it to cut us down. They already fly a drone along the big lines once a year instead of sending two of us walking. If that spreads to the small lines up the valley, they won't need four on a crew, they'll want three, and I'm not the one with the most years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get myself on the union committee at the depot so I'm in the room when they talk about it. I'd cancel the gym and stop eating at the café by the depot to put fifty a week aside, because I've got nothing behind me. I wouldn't go chasing courses on drones. I'm not a computer person and I'd be bad at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because people still have work in this one, but I'd be watching every email from the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, our oldest climber. He's fifty-six and he can read a pole by knocking it, but he's never touched a tablet. If the new way means flying drones and reading screens, they'll push him out first, and then it's me next, because I'm the same with screens, just younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the drones, but you also think they're coming. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know how that sounds. I'd rather fight for the job I know than be the worst person on a course I hate. Maybe that's stubborn, but I've seen what happens to blokes who chase every new thing. The company drops them anyway.

S1.say: We need it in writing that no drone replaces a crew and nobody is let go over new kit. I'd tell mates to join the union and share its posts, but not write my own.
S1.think: The company would use it to cut crews from four to three, starting with drone patrols on the valley lines. He isn't the most senior, so he'd be at risk early.
S1.do: Joins the depot union committee so he's in the room for any talks about new equipment. Cancels the gym and stops eating at the café to put about fifty a week aside, but doesn't sign up for drone courses.
S1.feel: Anxious and watchful, though not panicked, because most people still have work.
S1.quote: Maybe that's stubborn, but I've seen what happens to blokes who chase every new thing. The company drops them anyway.
S1.fieldNote: He openly admits the contradiction: he expects drones to spread but won't learn them. His answer is collective protection, not personal upskilling. The worry about older colleague Pete shows he thinks of the crew as one unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud for once. I'd say the government has to stop the power company from replacing crews until there's a plan for the people. I'd be at every union meeting and probably at a protest outside head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I don't know if a robot can do a pole change on a hill farm in sleet in two years. I really doubt it. But if it can, and it's cheaper, then I've got under a month of money, a partner whose care job is probably going too, and no other line company within seventy kilometres. That's not a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop every spare cost, sell the motorbike I hardly ride, and get that money in the bank, maybe two thousand. I'd push the union to demand full pay for anyone pushed out until there's something else. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect wages, and if it came to it, I'd ask Rosa's mum if we could move back in with her for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when you hear a crack on a pole you're already strapped to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell the bike, that's the first weekend. Then sit down with Rosa and actually write out what we spend, which we've never done. I'd rather know the bad number than keep guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been skint before and we got through it. She'd probably be more worried about her residents than about us, that's what she's like. I don't think I'd tell her how scared I was.

S2.say: The government has to stop the power company replacing crews until there's a plan for the people. He'd be at every union meeting and protest outside head office.
S2.think: He doubts robots can change poles on hill farms in sleet within two years, but if they can, he has under a month's money, a partner whose care job may also go, and no other line employer nearby.
S2.do: Sells his motorbike in the first weekend, puts about two thousand in the bank and cuts every spare cost. Pushes the union to demand full pay for anyone pushed out, votes for wage protection and would ask Rosa's mother about moving in.
S2.feel: Sick with fear, which he would hide from his partner.
S2.quote: I'd rather know the bad number than keep guessing.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario that makes a quiet man loud. He hangs on to doubt that robots could manage rural poles so fast, but plans as if they could. He would keep his fear from Rosa, and that private gap stood out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same as with the fast one, but with more planning behind it. I'd say five years is enough time for the government and the company to sit down with the union and agree what happens to us. I'd say that at work and I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years isn't much for me. I'm twenty-seven, so at thirty-two I'm out of a trade and starting from nothing. But at least you could see it coming, and the union would have time to win something, like a payout per year worked, or retraining that's actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, a set amount on payday before I can touch it, even if it's just eighty a month. I'd be on the committee pushing for a written deal. If they offered paid retraining, I'd take it, but it would have to be something hands-on, maybe looking after the robots themselves, not sitting in front of a screen all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. It's the same cliff, it's just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm just scrambling. Five years, I could get the union to fight for something real and maybe get a bit of money behind me. It's the same cliff, but with five years at least I can see where the edge is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take paid retraining. Earlier you said you'd be bad on a course. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. If it's paid and the alternative is nothing, I'd do it and probably hate it. I'd still be the slowest one in the room with the tablets, I know that.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for the government and the company to sit down with the union and agree what happens to lineworkers. He'd say the same at work and at the pub.
S3.think: At thirty-two he'd be out of a trade and starting over, but with warning the union could win a payout per year worked or properly paid retraining.
S3.do: Sets up an automatic saving of about eighty a month on payday and pushes on the committee for a written deal. Would take paid retraining if it's hands-on, such as maintaining the robots.
S3.feel: Uneasy turning into anxious, because the threat is the same but further off.
S3.quote: It's the same cliff, but with five years at least I can see where the edge is.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns panic into a negotiating plan. He still sees himself as bad with screens, yet would accept paid retraining when the alternative is nothing. He measures every option by whether it's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse if workers get dumped. I'd say the company owes us a plan, written down, years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like forever and like nothing at the same time. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd probably keep climbing for most of it, because the hill lines will be the last thing they automate, and I'd hope something comes along before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep the savings going, slowly. I'd stay on the union committee and push for the company to start a fund now for people like me. If there was a decent apprentice trainer job going in eight years or so, teaching the basics before the robots take over, I'd go for that, because it's still in the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like knowing your knees will go one day. You live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any plans with Rosa, like having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it would. We've talked about kids in a couple of years. If I knew my job had ten years left, I'm not sure I'd want a baby at thirty, then be out of work at thirty-seven with a seven-year-old. I'd hate that a robot I've never seen gets a vote on whether we have a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Probably wait a year or two and see what the union gets. That's not a great answer, but it's the honest one.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse if workers get dumped. The company owes lineworkers a written plan, years ahead.
S4.think: He'd be thirty-seven at the end and would probably keep climbing most of the decade, since hill lines would be last to go, hoping something turns up.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving slowly, stays on the union committee and pushes the company to start a transition fund now. Holds off on starting a family for a year or two to see what the union wins.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like knowing your knees will give out one day and living with it.
S4.quote: I'd hate that a robot I've never seen gets a vote on whether we have a kid.
S4.fieldNote: The longest timeline doesn't make him plan for a new career. It makes him wait and lean harder on the union. The surprise was how directly it reached into family plans: a robot getting 'a vote' on whether they have a child.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There's no time to save, no time for the union to win anything, and nowhere else around here to go. What would help is a law that says if they bring in robots, the people they replace keep most of their pay for a few years and get paid training. And a real raise now, so I'm not starting from zero.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who decides. Nobody's asking the blokes on the poles. The people buying the robots have never been up a pole at three in the morning with the wind going. They should have to talk to us first.

headlineQuote: The people buying the robots have never been up a pole at three in the morning with the wind going.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old distribution lineworker on a four-person crew covering hill farms and valley villages, about seven years into the trade. He lives with his partner Rosa, a night carer, and they have almost nothing saved after rent and the cost of the van he needs to reach the depot. He doesn't use AI and doesn't want to, and he'd rather fight for his job through the union than retrain on technology he expects to be bad at. He shrugs off AI Plateau, gets anxious at Steady Disruption, and is badly shaken by AGI by 2028, while the longer timelines turn his fear into union demands and a hesitation about having children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to save, no time for the union to win anything, and no other line work nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing that workers replaced by robots keep most of their pay for a few years and get paid training, plus a real pay rise now so he isn't starting from zero.
